author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your courier has informed me of the capture of Dominica. My Toulon squadron sailed on the 9th (Germinal), or thirteen days ago, and I have no news of it. It had a division on board under the command of Lauriston. The English are in a bad way in India. […]”

context: Italy armed for the coming war.
tweet: Your courier tells me Dominica fell. My Toulon squadron sailed a fortnight ago with Lauriston's division; no news yet. England bleeds in India; Decaen arms the Mahrattas with guns and officers. A Walcheren venture is madness.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “An expedition to Walcheren is absurd. I shall always 25 repent having listened in the year XI. to General Monnet, and having lost a number of men by sickness. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Lyons. To Marmont: Walcheren absurd; Monnet cost men by sickness.
tweet: Dominica is ours; my Toulon squadron sailed with Lauriston, and Decaen arms the Mahrattas in India. But Walcheren is absurd — I shall always repent Monnet sickly losses. Keep no Frenchmen there.

displayText: “I beg you will inform M. de Moustier that I cannot conceive how a man of so much judgment allows 30,000 Russians to alarm him for Prussia which has 300,000 men. The artillery, cavalry, and officers of the Prussian army are worth thirty times those of Russia. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Jerome Bonaparte May 6, i8o. "Jerome is wrong to think that he will be able to count upon any weakness on my par% for, not having the rights of a father, I cannoc entertain for him the feeling of a father; a father allows himself to be blinded, and it pleases him to be blinded because he identifies his son with himself. context: Jérôme's American marriage forbidden.
tweet: Jerome fancies some weakness in me will indulge him. Having no father's rights, I bear no father's blind love; a father loves being blind, seeing himself in his son. I cannot be blinded where duty rules. Let him earn, not presume.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The coronation took place yesterday with pomp. The church was splendid. The ceremony passed off as well as that in Paris, with this difference, that the weather was superb. […]”

tweet: Brother-in-law — this Anglo-Russian alliance talk is English-spread nonsense, utterly false, to wriggle from their straits. I know the truth, but the country alarms easily.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother-in-law and Cousin, — What you write to me concerning the conclusion of a treaty of alliance between England and Russia is nonsense; it is entirely false. These reports, spread by the English so that they may for the moment escape from their difficulties, are unfounded. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Milan: the Iron Crown taken.
tweet: Sir, my Brother-in-law and Cousin, what you write concerning the conclusion of a treaty of alliance between England and Russia is nonsense; it is entirely false. These reports, spread by the English so that they may for the moment escape from their difficulties, are unfounded.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Have several letters printed in the papers, as if from St. Petersburg, declaring that the French are much better treated; that court and town feel the necessity of making friends with us; that all are persuaded English avidity is the real cause of the war; that the English are unpopular; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris held while Italy crowns.
tweet: I want letters printed as from Petersburg: Frenchmen well used there, court and town for friendship, English greed blamed for the war, their coalition broken, Russia still.

tweet: I hear Genoa would join us — England alone objects. As for Fouché Anglo-Russian treaty: false, a failed English ruse. Though Pitt proclaim it in Parliament, call it untrue.

FOUCH. " Milan, 29 May, 1805. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But I know not, in truth, what kind of precaution will protect her from the terrible chance she runs. A nation is very foolish when it has no fortifications and no army to lay itself open to seeing an army of 100,000 veteran troops land on its shores. […]”

tweet: Keep sending me the Seleucia archbishop Rome-to-Dresden letters — my decipherers read them easy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I wish you to embark the artillery, powder, and all the ammunitions, so that in twenty-four bours the whole expedition may start. A general of brigade, with some dashing officers, should embark with Marshal Ney's corps, which will be the first to land. […]”

tweet: I want everything embarked — guns, powder, stores — within twenty-four hours. Ney lands first with a dashing vanguard; four beaches, no instant lost. Tell the marshals.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I think I ordered you to embark everything, for circumstances may present themselves at any moment. I wish you to embark the artillery, powder, and all the ammunitions, so that in twenty-four hours the whole expedition may start.

tweet: Spain gives me six Golden Fleeces — one is yours. Feed the Moniteur calming stories; my squadrons bring excellent news. Get two cardinals hats, and give Rayane and Caselli the Grand Eagle. Answer me on Jerome marriage.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This is necessary for all people, but especially for the 39 Italians, who only obey the voice of a master. They will esteem you only when they fear you, and they will fear you only when they see that you know their double and deceitful character. […]”

tweet: End the legislature by decree — it shall not meet under my reign. I thought too well of Italians; a third voted down a plain finance bill. No messages, no honours — publish my displeasure. They are not children, and there is malice in them.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All the news I receive from Italy is warlike, and Austria no longer conceals her intentions. Prepare a note for M. de Cobentzel, let it be long, wily, argumentative, and in similar terms to the inclosed. The note drawn up by Talleyrand was approved of, and forwarded to Vienna. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Decide now. Austria stalls with fine phrases to gain time and stop me achieving anything this year — her subsidy treaty signed, I shall find 100,000 Russians in Poland, 20,000 English at Malta, 15,000 Russians at Corfu. My mind is made up.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I decree horse races across the Empire, starting with the great breeding departments; prizes for the fleetest. The Orne, Correze, Seine, Morbihan, Sarre and Hautes-Pyrenees run yearly. I will improve the French horse.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As regards the encouragement of art, the Imperial Library being under the department. of the minister of the interior, and having placed 2oo,ooof. at his disposal,. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The camp breaks: administration turns toward the Rhine.
tweet: The Library answers to the interior minister, and I have placed 200,000 francs at his disposal — yet the treasury refuses to pay. David gets his sums, my librarian his engravings; the Gobelins and Sèvres must work without costing the treasury.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Sister, — I have ordered the grand marshal of my palace to send you my portrait, in accordance with your request, as you think it will be agreeable to the people of Lucca. Send me a detailed account of your coasts and a list of the batteries which are necessary. I will send you the guns. […]”
sourceTitle: To Princess Eliza, Camp  of  Boulogne, 1805-08-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Family principality news from camp.
tweet: My sister — the grand marshal sends my portrait for the people of Lucca, as you asked. Now send me a full account of your coasts with the batteries needed. I will send the guns.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The situation of my armies and the position of my forces do not permit of any transaction approaching to weakness. In giving Hanover to Prussia I give her a territory which will augment her forces to the extent of 40,000 men, and will also improve the situation of her states. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Boulogne to Rhine: the turn decided.
tweet: My armies admit no transaction smelling of weakness. Giving Hanover to Prussia augments her by 40,000 men and improves her states — in return she guarantees my Italy and Tuscany, and my Rhine frontier stands.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “With thirty vessels my admirals ought not to be afraid of twenty-four English ships, or else we must give up the idea of having a marine. If Villeneuve remains at Ferrol beyond the i6th, I shall consider him the last of men. According to the news from London, Nelson is still far away. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Villeneuve's fleet awaited in vain.
tweet: With thirty sail my admirals should not fear twenty-four English, or disband the navy. If Villeneuve idles at Ferrol past my deadline I call him the basest of men. London says Nelson roams far.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Third Coalition, September, i8o. " Soldiers: The war of the third coalition is commenced. The Austrian army has passed the Inn, violated treaties, attacked and driven our ally from his capital. You yourselves have been obliged to hasten, by forced marches, to the defence of our frontiers. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Third Coalition war proclaimed.
tweet: Soldiers, the third coalition's war is opened. Austria crossed the Inn, broke treaties, drove our ally from his capital. You yourselves were forced to double-march to our frontiers. They forced this war on us; answer with the courage that ever marks French arms.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have arrived at Strasburg. All the army has passed the Rhine. The enemy is at the issues of the Black Forest. Our manoeuvres will soon commence. Do all you can to induce the nation to adopt the conscription. " Napoleon.”

tweet: I have arrived at Strasburg. All the army has passed the Rhine. The enemy is at the issues of the Black Forest. Our manoeuvres will soon commence. Do all you can to induce the nation to adopt the conscription.

voice: Have it printed in the Gazettes that I am with the
tweet: Here are my German allies — Bavaria, Baden, Württemberg, Hesse-Darmstadt, all with strong corps. Print in the Gazettes that I am with the army and Austria flies in fear and disorder.

And all Villeneuve's crimes were recapitulated, including his conduct in not renewing his battle with Sir Robert Calder's disabled fleet, &c. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They hurried her into war. I groan over the blood which this will cost Europe; but the French name will obtain fresh lustre." The demands of Prussia, Austria, and Russia sufficiently explain the causes of this war. […]”

tweet: Tell priest Robert of Bourges I am displeased with his recent sermon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My dear and good brother of Austria came to Memmingen, but he appears to have returned to Vienna after having held a grand council. God grant that his army may remain in its present position for a week, or better still, that it may advance to the Rhine. […]”

tweet: My good Austrian brother came to Memmingen, counciled, and went home. God keep his army still a week — or better, marching on the Rhine. Woe to them if I gain a march or two.

context: Strasbourg. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: My only fear is lest we should frighten them too much.
voice: My only fear is lest we should frighten them too much
tweet: They hold the Black Forest passes — God keep them there. My only fear is frightening them off. Great things happen within a fortnight.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have made 60,000 prisoners, and taken 120 guns, 90 colours, and more than 30 generals. "I am going to march against the Russians; […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My good Josephine,— I have fatigued myself more than was prudent. All day long for a whole week wet to the skin, and the feet cold, have made me rather unwell; but I have not been out to-day, and that has rep'osed me. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The two last nights have rested me much, and I shall leave to-morrow for Munich. I send for M. de Talleyrand and M. de Maret" to be near me. I shall see them but little. T go 1 Talleyrand was then Minister of Foreign Affairs. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have attacked the Russians but lightly, for no matter how quickly we march, they retire more quickly still. […]”

context: Linz. To M. Cambacfires: I have received your letter, and beg you will thank the Council of State.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think there will be no inconvenience in your coming to meet me at the Abbaye de Moelk. You can pass by Braunau where you will see General Lauriston. The Emperor of Germany is still at Vienna. He has written me several letters, and would like to come to an arrangement. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Art I. A contribution of ioo,ooo,ooof shall be raised in Moravia and the other provinces of the House of Austria occupied by the French army. " Art. 2. This sum is to be given as a recompense to the army. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Emperor Of Russia, Headquarters, 1805-11-02

context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To Tsar Alexander: Moravia taxed for the army.
tweet: I lay my War contribution on Moravia and occupied Austria — this sum rewards the army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sire, — I send my aide-de-camp. General Savary, to your Majesty in order to compliment you on your arrival. I have charged him to assure you of all my esteem, and of my desire to find opportunities of proving how ambitious I am to win your friendship. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Emperor of Russia, Linz, 1805-11-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: A letter to the Tsar before the shock.
tweet: Sire, I send Savary, my aide, to greet your arrival. I charge him to avow my esteem and my hunger for chances to prove how I covet your friendship. Receive him with your famed kindness, and count me foremost among those who would please you.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I write to M. d'Harville in order that you set out, and that you proceed to Baden, from thence to Stuttgard, and from there to Munich. You will give at Stuttgard the wedding present to the Princess Paul. It is sufficient that it cost fifteen to twenty thousand francs ($3000 to $4000). […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Their force consisted of 80,000 Russians and 30,000 Austrians. I have made about 40,000 prisoners, taken 40. […]”

context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To his brother Joseph: I have made about 40,000 prisoners, taken 40.
voice: I have made about 40,000 prisoners, taken 40
tweet: Yesterday I fought the decisive battle. 80,000 Russians and 30,000 Austrians stood against my smaller army — I took 40,000 prisoners, their cannon, their standards. Tonight I sleep in Kaunitz's castle, in a clean shirt for the first time in eight days.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The widows of colonels and majors, 2,400 francs; the widows of captains, 1,200 francs; the widows of lieutenants, 800 francs; the widows of soldiers, 200 francs. And by another dec […]”
sourceTitle: To The Elector Of Vvirtemberg, AUSTERLITZ, 1805-12-01

tweet: Dolgorouki came to my outposts oozing arrogance — mistook my moderation for fear. That error gave me Austerlitz. Now the Tsar has opened his eyes and wants peace, never to meddle again.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the anniversary of my coronation, that day upon which the Holy Father, the cardinals, and all the 87 clergy of France, offered up prayers in the sanctuary of Notre Dame for the prosperity of our reign. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Cardinal Archbishop Of Paris, BRTJNN, 1805-12-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To his uncle Cardinal Fesch: We have taken forty-five flags from the enemy.
tweet: We have taken forty-five flags. On this anniversary of my coronation — the day the Holy father and all 87 clergy of France prayed for my reign at Notre Dame — I will hang them in the church. Paris shall see them.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Before driving Austria to extremities and attacking Naples, it was necessary to have some assurance that the Cabinet of Berlin would not suddenly change its tone, and that no danger was to be expected from that quarter. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To Marshal Davout: Before driving Austria to extremities and attacking Naples, it was necessary to have some assurance that the Cabinet of Berlin would not suddenly change its tone…
tweet: Davout — send me a detailed, truthful account of Austerlitz. Tell me plainly what happened, and whether Klein's division did anything.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A million francs in paper will be placed at your disposal. " You will propose a plan for distributing two millions among the marshals, generals, and colonels. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Orders after the victory.
tweet: Berthier — a million in paper is at your disposal. Bring me a plan for distributing two millions among my marshals, generals and colonels.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I have arrived at Munich. I have arranged your marriage with the Princess Augusta. The banns have been published. This morning the princess paid me a visit, and I had a long conversation with her. You will find her portrait on the accompanying cup; but she is much better. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy secured by the Danube victory.
tweet: Eugène — I have arranged your marriage with Princess Augusta of Bavaria. The banns are published; she visited me this morning, and she is even lovelier than her portrait.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Besides, everything here has been sent away or sold, with the exception of 500 or 600 guns. If you cannot sign peace at once, wait and sign it on the advent of the new year; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Besides, everything here has been sent away or sold, with the exception of 500 or 600 guns.
tweet: Your letter is here. The Emperor and Charles both write — I meet the archduke three leagues from Vienna. I congratulated peace but concede nothing; no politics with Charles, two hours: one dining, one soldiering.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother,— I have received your letter of the 20th Frimaire. Negotiations continue; my army is reposing. The army of Prince Charles is close here. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Austerlitz eve, from imperial headquarters.
tweet: My brother, yours received. Talks drag on; my army rests. Charles's host lies close. Likely, if peace lags, within weeks comes a stroke leaving Austria not a shadow of resource. I wait, ready.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 3rd Nivose. The Emperor and Prince Charles have written to me. I shall have an interview with the archduke at three leagues from Vienna. I send you a copy of my letter to the Emperor, who has written to me in the most amiable manner. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Eve of battle diplomacy.
tweet: I have received your letter of the Nivose. The Emperor and Prince Charles have written to me. I shall have an interview with the archduke at three leagues from Vienna. I send you a copy of my letter to the Emperor, who has written to me in the most amiable manner.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am satisfied with you. In the Battle of Austerlitz you have justified all that I expected from your intrepidity. You have decorated your eagles with immortal glory. An army of one hundred thousand men, commanded by the Emperors of Russia and Austria, has been, in less than four hours, either cut in pieces or dispersed. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: 'I am satisfied with you': the bulletin-proclamation.
tweet: I am satisfied with you. In the battle of Austerlitz you have justified all that I expected from your intrepidity. You have decorated your eagles with immortal glory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have dispatched Lebrun to you from the field of battle. I have beaten the Austrian and Russian armies commanded by the two Emperors. I am a little fatigued. I have bivouacked eight days in the open air, through some very cold nights. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “After manoeuvring for a few days I fought a decisive battle yesterday. I defeated the combined armies commanded by the Emperors of Russia and of Germany. Their force consisted of 80,000 Russians and 30,000 Austrians. I have made about 40,000 prisoners, taken 40. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have concluded a truce. The Russians have gone home again. The battle of Austerlitz is the most glorious of all which I have gained. Forty-five stands of colors, more than one hundred and fifty pieces of cannon, the banners of the Russian guard, twenty generals, thirty thousand prisoners, […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Truce concluded; Russians going home.
tweet: I have concluded a truce. The Russians have gone home again. The battle of Austerlitz is the most glorious of all which I have gained.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I Lave concluded an armistice. Before eight days, peace will be made. I hope to learn that you have arrived at Munich, in good health. The Russians have retired. They have sustained an immense loss; more than twenty thousand killed and thirty thousand taken. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Armistice; peace within eight days.
tweet: I have concluded an armistice. Before eight days, peace will be made. I hope to learn that you have arrived at Munich, in good health. The Russians have retired. They have sustained an immense loss; more than twenty thousand killed and thirty thousand taken.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Napoleon, however, was inexorable, caring little for that revenge which his enemy would be driven to seek on the first opportunity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: The Emperor of Germany asked for an interview, which I granted.
tweet: The German Emperor had his interview — two to four, wanting peace on the spot, appealing to my feelings. I held firm — not hard. He has his armistice. Tell Haugwitz to wait at Vienna: victory hardens my terms, especially for negotiators sent the day of battle.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Ii. 204): — " From the opening of the campaign, pastorals had been published in every See justifying this new war, and calling upon the conscripts to join their corps. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The sun of Austerlitz: two emperors beaten in four hours. To his brother Joseph: Ii. — From the opening of the campaign, pastorals had been published in every See justifying this new war, and calling upon the conscripts to join their corps.
tweet: From this campaign opening, pastorals in every see justifying this new war, and calling upon the conscripts to join my corps.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Emperor of Germany asked for an interview, which I granted; it lasted from 2 till 4 P.M. I will. you what I think of him when I see you. He wished to conclude peace on the spot. He appealed to my feelings; I defended myself, a kind of warfare which I assure you was not difficult. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Austerlitz reported to diplomacy.
tweet: The Emperor of Germany asked for an interview, which I granted; it lasted from 2 till 4 P.M. I will tell you what I think of him when I see you. He wished to conclude peace on the spot.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Read Barbe-Marbois letter, seal it, deliver it. Incapacity or treason — the coalition never had a better ally. I suspend judgment till Paris, but he has surely betrayed me. One escape: restore the missing bonds. Talk finance, not Cambacérès.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother, — I send you a letter for the Minister of the Treasury (M. Barbe-Marbois). You will read it, then seal it and hand it to him. I do not yet know whether it is incapacity or treason, but the coalition has had no more useful ally than this minister. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — Despatch your brother, General Berthier, with the decree which nominates Prince Joseph commander-in-chief of the army of Naples. […]”

voice: @cambacirfes Despatch your brother, General Berthier, with the decree which nominates Prince Joseph commander-in-chief of the army of Naples
tweet: Despatch your brother Berthier with the decree making Joseph commander in Naples. He stays at headquarters in total secrecy — I am not sure Joseph will accept, so nothing must be known.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You are at perfect liberty to keep my minister at Rome or to send him away. The occupation of Ancona is the necessary consequence of the bad military organisation of the Holy See. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Prussia annihilated in seven days. To Pope Pius VII: Ancona held: Holy See can't defend it.
voice: @pope You are at perfect liberty to keep my minister at Rome or to send him away
tweet: Your letter grieved me deeply — while every Power in England pay leagues against me in an unjust war, you listened to bad counsels. Keep my minister or send him away, as you wish. But Ancona I hold: your fortress undefended, and better in my hands than the English.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is they who prostitute religion. Is there another example of an apostolic nuncio in Russia 1 Tell Consalvi — tell even the Pope — that since they wish to drive my minister from Rome, I may go there to reinstate him. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Munich. To his uncle Cardinal Fesch: Is there another example of an apostolic nuncio in Russia.
tweet: The Pope writes me letters both ridiculous and insane. I took Ancona because nothing was done for its defence — no bantering, no Russian ministers at Rome. I will replace you with a secular ambassador, even a Protestant one.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I have found your reflections upon Cardinal Rufifo very mean and puerile. You behave like a woman at Rome. You did wrong to advise the cardinal to come to Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his uncle Cardinal Fesch: You behave like a woman at Rome. You did wrong to advise the cardinal to come to Paris.
voice: @fesch I have found your reflections upon Cardinal Rufifo very mean and puerile
tweet: Your reflections on Rufifo are mean and puerile — you behave like a woman at Rome, meddling in what you do not understand. Take possession of the Venetian palace; I have written Joseph to aid you by force if need be.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I arrived here yesterday evening, and I shall leave to-morrow. I send you the Moniteur, in which you will find matters concerning yourself. " Napoleon. " P.S. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: New kingdoms ordered from Stuttgart.
tweet: My son — I arrived yesterday evening and leave again tomorrow. I send you the Moniteur with matters concerning yourself inside.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It was the conduct of my brother at the coronation and his refusal to accept the crown of Italy which made me call Eugene my son. I am determined to give the same title to another should he oblige me. […]”

voice: I am determined to give the same title to another should he oblige me
tweet: Your Placentia bulletin displeased me, but your measures satisfy me — I blame words and praise zeal. Marbois loses his portfolio; impossible deeds, though I still call him honest, led by scamps.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General St. Cyr another; and General Regnier the smallest, composed of 6,000 good troops in reserve. Make friends with General Regnier; he is cold, but of the three the most capable of drawing out a good plan of campaign and of giving you good advice. […]”

context: Munich. To his brother Joseph: Make friends with General Regnier; he is cold, but of the three the most capable of drawing out a good plan of campaign and of giving you good advice.
tweet: You will be near Rome soon; Dumas is sent. After rest you will hold 40,000 men in three corps — Massena strongest, St. Cyr, Regnier 6,000 reserve. Befriend cold Regnier; he plans best. Make each believe your confidence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will be in the vicinity of Rome on the 15th. I have sent you the General Dumas. Marshal Massena ought to be with the army. I count that after a few days' repose you will have 40,000 men, with whom you can form three corps: Marshal Massena will command the strongest; General St. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Pressburg peace: Austria pays, Naples falls to Joseph.
tweet: You will stand near Rome within days. I send Dumas; Massena should be there. After brief rest count forty thousand in three corps: Massena strongest, St Cyr another, Regnier a six-thousand reserve. Befriend cold Regnier; he plans best.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is only when you have united your whole army corps that you will demand 4,000,000 francs, and pay the same into the military chest of the Grand Army. " Napoleon." ' This was decreeing victory after the manner of the Convention. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will occupy Frankfort with a division of your army. At first you will levy no contribution on the city. It is only when you have united your whole army corps that you will demand 4,000,000 francs, and pay the same into the military chest of the Grand Army. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Marshals placed for peace.
tweet: Occupy Frankfort with one division, levying nothing yet. Only with your whole corps united will you demand four millions for the Grand Army's chest. I decree victory beforehand, after the Convention's fashion.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As M. Haugwitz has not yet made his appearance see that my army remains ready for war, and to act with the rapidity of thought. And the army did remain ready until it was wanted to punish Prussian tergiversations and weakness, and to march on Berlin. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his chief of staff Berthier: As M. Haugwitz has not yet made his appearance see that my army remains ready for war, and to act with the rapidity of thought.
voice: As M. Haugwitz has not yet made his appearance see that my army remains ready for war, and to act with the rapidity of thought
tweet: Your letters are here — Munich, I presume. Till Haugwitz shows, keep my army ready for war, ready to move at the speed of thought.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I can understand nothing of all this. Let Prince Eugene send you troops. Burn five or six villages, and shoot some sixty persons; make very severe examples, for the consequences of what is passing in Parma are incalculable for the security of Italy. […]”

tweet: I can make nothing of this Parma business. Send Eugène's troops, burn five or six villages, shoot sixty men — make examples so severe Italy learns its lesson. And where is Menou in all this?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Emperor will support with all his influence, and by force of arms, if necessary, all that the Prince of the Peace wishes to do with regard to Portugal. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Minister Of Foreign Affairs, Paris, 1806-02-01

tweet: 200,000 Prussians threaten — they are mad; tell Haugwitz this finishes. The prince of the peace has paid his 11,000,000 francs, and I will back him in Portugal by force of arms. Adventurers lie about Ireland; my eyes are on the navy until England makes peace.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I take the greatest interest in your prosperity, and especially in your glory, which, in your position, is of the first necessity; without it life can have no charm. I hope that Mathieu Dumas has joined you." Napoleon acted in his usual arbitrary manner in the Ouvrard affair. […]”

tweet: My cousin of Austria may remove the arms from his Tyrol castle — but see that François I's armour, and anything curious, is kept for me. I attach importance to it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Those who delay sending bulls to my bishops and who leave my dioceses in anarchy will have to answer for this before God. As for the affairs of Italy, I have done everything for the bishops; […]”

context: Paris. To his brother Joseph: As for the affairs of Italy, I have done everything for the bishops.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Disarm Naples, and levy a contribution of 10,000,000 francs on the city. It will be paid easily. You have certain resources by confiscating English merchandise. […]”

context: Paris. To his brother Joseph: Disarm Naples, and levy a contribution of 10,000,000 francs on the city.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Sister,— I beg that you will allow your Court to wear nothing but silks and cambric, and that you will exclude all cottons and muslins in order to favour French industry. […]”
